One: the class takes a database handle in its constructor and never imports the global pool, which is what lets a test hand it a transaction that is rolled back afterwards. Two: every public method returns domain objects built by one private function at the bottom of the file, so column names appear in exactly one place. Three: methods that write accept an optional transaction and otherwise open their own; nothing commits on behalf of a caller. Four: lists take a cursor and a limit and return the items plus the next cursor, using the shared helper, never an offset. The tests take 6 and a half minutes on a single runner; they are already independent of each other, so splitting them over three runners would bring that to a little over 2 minutes plus start-up. The build takes about 2 minutes and only needs to run when the earlier stages pass. Walk me through what happens to a request between the socket and the route handler. I keep losing track of which middleware runs when, and I need to know before I add anything new to that chain.

In order, for every request. First the server assigns a request id and starts a timer. Second, the body parser reads JSON bodies up to 1 MB and rejects anything larger with a 413 before any of our code sees it. Third, the authentication middleware looks for the API key in the Authorization header, loads the key record through the repository layer and attaches the account to the request; a missing or unknown key ends the request with a 401 here. Fourth, the validation middleware checks the path, query and body against the schema that the route declared and answers 422 with the list of problems when they do not match. Fifth, the route handler runs and returns a plain object. Sixth, on the way out, the serializer turns that object into JSON, the timer stops, and one line is written with the request id, the status and the time taken. An error thrown anywhere jumps to the error handler, which maps known error classes to their status codes and turns everything else into a 500 without leaking the message. So a new middleware that needs the account must sit after the third step, and one that must see every request, even rejected ones, must sit before it. tail.text: How do credentials reach the pipeline when I run it locally? I do not want to paste anything into my shell history.

Locally the pipeline never reads credentials from the command line. It asks the keyring of the operating system for an entry named tidewater-local, and when that entry does not exist it uses the stand-in database and the sample files, which need no credentials at all. So the default local run is safe by construction: without the keyring entry nothing can reach a real system. To work against the staging warehouse you store the entry once with the tw login command, which asks for the value on a prompt that does not echo and writes it only to the keyring. Production is not reachable from a local run in any case: the client refuses the production address unless it runs under the scheduler identity. Nothing needs to be pasted into a shell, and nothing changed in the code; this is how pipeline/credentials.py works today.
How are the sample folders produced? I want a fourth one with returns in it and I do not want to build it by hand.

The samples come from tools/make_samples.py. It takes a seed, a number of orders and a "shape" and writes a folder of files in the same layout as the real feed, with invented customers and products. The shape decides the mix: small makes 200 orders with one to three lines each, medium makes 20,000 with the same mix, and wide makes 300 orders with up to 400 lines each to stress the line parser. Every run with the same seed gives the same files, byte for byte, which is what keeps the tests stable. Returns are not generated today: the script has a place for them, a function that is declared and raises "not implemented". A fourth shape would need that function written, which means deciding what share of orders is returned and after how many days, and writing the returns file in the layout the feed documentation describes. It is perhaps fifty lines. I have not written it; tell me the share and the delay you want and I will add the shape and a folder generated from it.
Suppose we get a new source table next quarter. What are the steps to bring it into the pipeline? I want to estimate the work.

Six steps, going by the document and by what the code really requires. One: describe the table in pipeline/registry.py with its name, key columns and the column that tells when a row changed. Two: write the staging definition under ddl/staging, key columns first. Three: write the transform, which is usually a list of column renames and type casts; only tables with nested data, such as order lines, need real code. Four: add the table to the row count check so that a load that loses rows is caught. Five: generate sample files for it and add at least the tests that every table has, which are a load of the small sample and a second load of the same sample that must change nothing. Six: add it to the scheduler job after the tables it depends on. For a flat table this is about a day including review. For a table with nested data, count three days, most of it in the transform and its tests. The document is accurate except that it does not mention the fourth step; I can add that paragraph if you like, but have not.

tail.text: I need to add a repository class for a new table next week. Show me the pattern by pointing at an existing one, so I copy the right things and not the historical accidents.

Use src/repositories/customers.ts as the model; it is the newest and the cleanest. The pattern has four parts. Four: lists take a cursor and a limit and return the items plus the next cursor, using the shared helper, never an offset. The historical accidents to leave behind are in the older files: a method there that returns raw rows, a cache that lives inside the repository, and a method that takes a whole request object. install 3 m 10 s, lint 1 m 05 s, types 1 m 40 s, test 6 m 30 s, build 1 m 50 s

Five stages, run one after another. Install takes a little over 3 minutes because the dependency cache is keyed on the commit, so it is never hit; keyed on the lockfile it would be hit on almost every run. Lint and the type check take about 1 and 2 minutes and do not depend on each other, so they could run side by side. The tests take 6 and a half minutes on a single runner; they are already independent of each other, so splitting them over three runners would bring that to a little over 2 minutes plus start-up. The build takes about 2 minutes and only needs to run when the earlier stages pass. Put together: caching on the lockfile, lint and types in parallel and three test runners would bring the pipeline from about 14 minutes to roughly 6, without removing any check. None of this is changed yet; it is the measurement of the last 20 runs and what follows from it. The cheapest single step is the cache key, which is a one-line change in the pipeline file.
Walk me through what happens to a request between the socket and the route handler. I keep losing track of which middleware runs when, and I need to know before I add anything new to that chain.

In order, for every request. First the server assigns a request id and starts a timer. Second, the body parser reads JSON bodies up to 1 MB and rejects anything larger with a 413 before any of our code sees it. Third, the authentication middleware looks for the API key in the Authorization header, loads the key record through the repository layer and attaches the account to the request; a missing or unknown key ends the request with a 401 here. Fourth, the validation middleware checks the path, query and body against the schema that the route declared and answers 422 with the list of problems when they do not match. Fifth, the route handler runs and returns a plain object. Sixth, on the way out, the serializer turns that object into JSON, the timer stops, and one line is written with the request id, the status and the time taken. An error thrown anywhere jumps to the error handler, which maps known error classes to their status codes and turns everything else into a 500 without leaking the message. So a new middleware that needs the account must sit after the third step, and one that must see every request, even rejected ones, must sit before it. I changed nothing; this is a description of src/server.ts as it is.

tail.text: Walk me through what happens to a request between the socket and the route handler. I keep losing track of which middleware runs when, and I need to know before I add anything new to that chain.

In order, for every request. First the server assigns a request id and starts a timer. Second, the body parser reads JSON bodies up to 1 MB and rejects anything larger with a 413 before any of our code sees it. Third, the authentication middleware looks for the API key in the Authorization header, loads the key record through the repository layer and attaches the account to the request; a missing or unknown key ends the request with a 401 here. Fourth, the validation middleware checks the path, query and body against the schema that the route declared and answers 422 with the list of problems when they do not match. Fifth, the route handler runs and returns a plain object. Sixth, on the way out, the serializer turns that object into JSON, the timer stops, and one line is written with the request id, the status and the time taken. An error thrown anywhere jumps to the error handler, which maps known error classes to their status codes and turns everything else into a 500 without leaking the message. So a new middleware that needs the account must sit after the third step, and one that must see every request, even rejected ones, must sit before it. 4. Files and code sections: pipeline/extract.py (watermark query), pipeline/load.py (batching, the resend after a timeout near line 88), pipeline/transform.py (line item parser), checks/row_counts.sql (staging against warehouse), docs/runbooks/nightly-load.md (what to do when a nightly load fails), ddl/staging (three files, columns sorted), tests/test_line_items.py (38 cases), utils/dates.py (type errors fixed).
5. Errors met and how they were handled: a deprecation warning in the transform step (the option was removed); three type errors in the date helpers (fixed without behaviour change); a slow pre-commit hook (explained, not changed).

Continuing after the summary. Nothing is in flight, so I wait for your next instruction.
The type checker is unhappy with the helpers in utils/dates.py. Can you look? No behaviour change please.

utils/dates.py:22: error: Returning Any from function declared to return "date"
Found 3 errors in 1 file
Success: no issues found in 1 source file

The three type errors in utils/dates.py are gone. They all came from one helper that returned the result of a parse call without saying what type it is; it now checks the type before returning. Behaviour is the same: the 12 tests of the date helpers pass unchanged.
Suppose we get a new source table next quarter. What are the steps to bring it into the pipeline? I want to estimate the work.

Six steps, going by the document and by what the code really requires. One: describe the table in pipeline/registry.py with its name, key columns and the column that tells when a row changed. Two: write the staging definition under ddl/staging, key columns first. Three: write the transform, which is usually a list of column renames and type casts; only tables with nested data, such as order lines, need real code. Four: add the table to the row count check so that a load that loses rows is caught. Five: generate sample files for it and add at least the tests that every table has, which are a load of the small sample and a second load of the same sample that must change nothing. Six: add it to the scheduler job after the tables it depends on. For a flat table this is about a day including review. For a table with nested data, count three days, most of it in the transform and its tests. The document is accurate except that it does not mention the fourth step; I can add that paragraph if you like, but have not.
Rename the log field "dur" to "duration_ms" in the step logger, the dashboards people keep asking what dur means.

pipeline/log.py:31
pipeline/log.py:58

The step logger writes duration_ms instead of dur now, in both places where it was set. The value is the same number of milliseconds as before. Saved searches that filter on dur will need the new name; I found two of them in the dashboards folder and listed them in the commit message, but did not edit the dashboards.
Is there a quick way to run one step locally against the sample files?

Yes: make step STEP=transform SAMPLE=samples/small runs a single step against a folder of sample files and writes its output to out/local. It uses the local SQLite stand-in for the warehouse, so nothing leaves your machine. The three sample folders are small (200 orders), medium (20,000) and wide (few orders with many line items). The command prints the row counts of the step at the end, the same ones a real run writes to its log.
Fix the resend in the loader now.
7 passed in 0.48s

The loader no longer resends a batch after a timeout: it first asks the warehouse whether the load_id of that batch was already written and only sends it again when it was not. Seven tests cover the timeout cases.
Sort the columns in the staging DDL files alphabetically after the key columns, it makes diffs easier to read.

The three staging DDL files now list the key columns first and every other column in alphabetical order. This changes only the text of the files: the column order of the existing tables is untouched, and no migration is needed because the staging tables are created fresh on each run.
The unit tests take a minute and a half, which is long for what they do. See whether something silly is going on.
94.2s total; setup of db fixture: 0.38s x 214 tests
214 passed in 21.6s

Something silly was going on: the fixture that provides the local stand-in database created a new database file and ran every definition file for each single test, 214 times, at about 0.4 seconds each. Most tests only read from it. The fixture now builds the database once per test module and gives each test a transaction that is rolled back at the end, so tests still cannot see each other's rows. The run went from 94 seconds to under 22, with the same 214 tests passing. Three tests needed their own fresh database because they test the definition files themselves; they ask for it explicitly now through a second fixture. Nothing outside the tests folder changed.
Add a small test for the helper that turns a file name into a load date.
5 passed in 0.21s

Added tests/test_load_date.py with five cases: a plain name, a name with a sequence suffix, a name with an upper-case extension, a name without a date (expects an error) and a date that does not exist such as 31 February (expects an error). All five pass.
Read the README of the pipeline as if you were new here and tell me what is wrong with it. Fix what is plainly out of date, leave questions of taste to me.

Read as a newcomer, three things were plainly out of date and are fixed. The install section named a requirements file that no longer exists; it now names the lock file and the one command that installs from it. The section on running a step used the old command name; it now shows the make target with the STEP and SAMPLE variables. The list of folders was missing tools and checks and still listed a notebooks folder that was deleted in the summer. Two things are matters of taste and are untouched: the README opens with the history of the project rather than with what the pipeline does, and the troubleshooting section is longer than everything else together. One thing is missing and I did not invent it: there is no word on who to ask when a run fails outside working hours.
Why does the transform step print a warning about a deprecated option on every run?
DeprecationWarning: the "infer_datetime" option is deprecated

The warning came from an option of the CSV reader that its library has deprecated; the transform step passed it explicitly although its value was the default. I removed the option, so the warning is gone and the parsed result is identical: I compared the output of the medium sample before and after, byte for byte.
